sens: Further than, on the other side of
G1900.detail: 1. The word designates what is found on the other side of a limit, beyond a border or a landmark. In Acts 7:43, Peter announces that God will transport the people "beyond Babylon" — beyond the known place of exile, even further, into Assyria. It is the image of surpassing a location, going beyond.
G1900.origine: The word comes from the preposition "epi" (on, towards) combined with "ekaina" (that side), literally forming "towards what is on the other side." This construction expresses movement beyond a limit or a point of reference. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses the word "halah" (הָלְאָה) to express the same idea: what exceeds, what is further away.
G1900.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 7:43, in Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin. Stephen quotes the prophet Amos to remind the people that they worshiped idols in the desert. The phrase "will I transport you beyond Babylon" announces a punishment: an exile that would go beyond even the known place of exile. It is a prophetic threat — not just exile to Babylon, but an even more distant dispersion.
G1900.portee: This word reminds us that the consequences of sin can exceed what we imagine: God's judgment does not stop where we think it does. It is also an invitation to take the warnings of the prophets seriously — God follows through on His words to the end.

sens: To stretch towards something, to extend arms or body in a direction
To make an effort to achieve a distant goal, to mentally project oneself forward
To resolutely turn towards a goal, to engage all one's strength towards it
G1901.detail:
1. The verb first evokes a physical gesture: one stretches forward, extending limbs to reach what is in front. It is the image of an athlete leaning towards the finish line.
2. Paul uses it in a spiritual and moral sense in Philippians 3:13: "reaching out for what is ahead." He describes the believer's effort to leave behind his past (his mistakes, weaknesses, what he has already accomplished) and turns with all his being towards the goal — Jesus Christ and the heavenly reward.
3. It is a movement of total commitment: not a simple weak desire, but an active tension, a fervent appetite. The believer does not remain still; he leaps forward.
G1901.origine: The word is formed from three elements: "epi" (towards, on), "ek" (out of, from) and "teinô" (to stretch, to extend). This composition reinforces the idea of energetic extension forward. The root image is that of muscular extension, the deployment of force. The Greek word reveals a posture of active pursuit, very different from a simple passive aspiration.
G1901.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 3:13, where Paul speaks of his own spiritual life. He uses the means (that is, he says "I reach out towards" rather than "I carry towards"), which emphasizes that it is an act engaging his whole person. This unique context is one of exhortation to the Philippians: living the Christian life is not looking back with regret or satisfaction, but projecting oneself body and soul towards the final goal. The uniqueness of the word makes it all the more striking: Paul chooses a rare and dynamic expression to describe the conversion of heart and effort.
G1901.portee: This word speaks to the believer about the authenticity of conversion: believing in Christ means turning away from the past and walking with all one's being towards Him. It invites us to examine the true orientation of our heart — are we really reaching out towards Jesus and eternal life, or are we still attached to what is behind? It is also a call to perseverance: the Christian path requires tension, a constant but joyful effort.

sens: to put a garment over another
to have an additional garment on oneself
figuratively: to cover oneself with, to envelop oneself in something added
to obtain a heavenly body that envelops and transforms the earthly body
G1902.detail:
1. The literal meaning of the word is to put a garment over another: "to put on over." It is the idea of something that adds, that superimposes on what one already has. The preposition "epi" (on) joined with the verb "enduo" (to put on) creates this precise image: it is not replacing, it is adding on top.

2. In the passive sense, it is "to have on oneself" an additional garment, to be clothed with something added. The image is that of an added layer that envelops and protects.

3. Paul uses it figuratively to express a deep desire: to be "clothed" with a heavenly dwelling (2 Corinthians 5:2). This is not a simple change of clothes, but a transformation that covers and transforms our entire existence.

4. In the same passage (2 Corinthians 5:4), this "clothing" means the acquisition of a resurrected and glorified body that would envelop our current mortal condition — not to leave us naked, but to be transformed and enveloped by eternal and indestructible life.
G1902.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "enduo" (to put on, to dress) to which the preposition "epi" (on) is added. This composition emphasizes the idea of adding on top, of superimposing. The family of words of this type always evokes the act of covering, enveloping one's body with clothing or, figuratively, with qualities. It is a common Greek word, attested among Greek historians.
G1902.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both occurrences found in 2 Corinthians 5:2-4. Paul uses it in an eschatological context to express the hope of Christians. He plays on the contrast: we groan in our earthly body like in a temporary tent; we do not wish to "be unclothed" (to die without resurrection), but to "put on" — that is, to receive a glorified body that would envelop and transform our mortal condition. The term therefore expresses not complete exchange, but transformation by addition, by new covering. This image of "clothing" makes palpable Paul's desire for a transformed continuity, not for annihilation.
G1902.portee: For the believer, this word crystallizes the Easter hope: we are not called to disappear or to become disembodied spirits, but to be transformed and enveloped in a new, glorious, and indestructible life. It is a promise of transfigured continuity — our identity and our body are not erased, but covered and renewed by the power of God. This language of Jesus speaks directly to our desire to live fully, without losing our embodiment or our humanity.

sens: Tunic or coat worn over other clothing
Outer layer of clothing added for covering
G1903.detail:
1. A garment worn over the ordinary tunic, what we would call a coat, cape, or overcoat. It is a garment that could be easily put on and taken off, distinct from the tunic worn directly on the skin. In John 21:7, Peter, who had stripped off his clothes to work at fishing (he was 'naked'), first puts on this outer garment before jumping into the water to go to Jesus — an act that shows one could not present oneself before someone without this minimum of dignity.

2. By extension, the word refers to the outer layer that covers and protects. This is why the Old Testament used it for the robe of the high priest (מְעִיל, the sacred garment worn by Aaron) or the clothing that kings and prophets wore as a sign of authority. It is less a simple garment than a clothing that 'envelops' and 'exposes' the one who wears it.
G1903.origine: The Greek word ἐπενδύτης (ependutēs) comes from ἐπενδύω, which literally means 'to put over': ἐπί (upon, over) + ἐνδύω (to clothe, to dress). The image is that of something being put on or thrown over oneself. In Hebrew, the word מְעִיל (meîl) that it translates in the passages of the Greek Old Testament refers to the long and ample garment of the priest or king, a garment of display and responsibility. The Greek word generalizes this notion: it is any garment that is put 'over'.
G1903.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 21:7, where it describes Peter's garment while fishing. Peter was wearing an inner tunic (his work garment) and an outer garment that he could quickly take off and put on. When he recognizes Jesus, he puts on this garment as a sign of respect — a detail that shows Peter's humanity and the importance, in the culture of the time, of presenting oneself decently before someone. The word has no particular nuance: it is simply the technical term for this covering garment.
G1903.portee: This small detail in John 21:7 reminds us that faith is not abstract: Peter abandons his work, dignifies himself with his coat, and jumps into the water to run to meet Jesus. The garment he puts on symbolizes his respect and eagerness. It is also an invitation to consider the importance of restraint and dignity in our own relationship with God and with our brothers.

sens: To arrive, come to a place
To intervene suddenly or unexpectedly
To fall upon someone or something, speaking of misfortunes
To descend upon someone or something, speaking of an adversary
To come down, to manifest, speaking of the Holy Spirit or a power
G1904.detail:
1. The primary meaning is simply 'to arrive' at a place: Jews come from Antioch and Iconium to stone Paul (Acts 14:19). It is a movement that reaches its destination.

2. The verb often denotes a sudden and unexpected arrival or intervention: something that occurs without one really expecting it. This is why it is translated as 'to occur' rather than just 'to come'.

3. When misfortunes occur, it means they fall upon someone: terror will come upon the earth on the last day (Luke 21:26), calamities may occur upon the rich (James 5:1). The idea is one of an overwhelming arrival, difficult to avoid.

4. Applied to an enemy or adversary, the verb evokes an attack: a stronger one occurs and dominates the one who thought he was strong (Luke 11:22).

5. In spiritual passages, the verb expresses the descent or manifestation of a divine power: the Holy Spirit will come upon Mary (Luke 1:35), and the power of the Most High will descend upon her for the fulfillment of the mystery of the Incarnation.
G1904.origine: The word is composed of the preposition 'epi' (upon, at) and the verb 'erchomai' (to come, to go). The image is thus one of a coming 'upon' something or someone, an arrival that imposes itself or descends upon its target. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this verb often translates the verb 'bo'a' (to enter, to come) or 'abar' (to pass, to cross), with the idea of an irruption or invasion.
G1904.emploi: The verb appears 9 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Acts. It denotes either a simple movement (Acts 14:19) or the unexpected intervention of an outside force: an adversary (Luke 11:22), misfortunes or calamities (Luke 21:26; Acts 8:24; Acts 13:40; James 5:1), or a heavenly power (Luke 1:35; Acts 1:8; Ephesians 2:7). The nuance of meaning depends on the context: the word always emphasizes the aspect of an arrival that imposes itself or that one cannot control.
G1904.portee: This verb reminds us that the events of our lives—good or bad—do not depend entirely on us. The intervention of the Holy Spirit upon Mary, the invasion of fear on the last day, the sudden arrival of a temptation: all of this 'occurs'. This invites the Christian to vigilance, not to believe oneself autonomous, and to rely on the grace of God that can also 'occur' to help.

sens: To ask a question to someone to obtain an answer
To interrogate, to examine through questions
To solicit, to pray someone to do something
To challenge, to contest through a question
G1905.detail: 1. To ask means to pose a direct question to a person to learn something from them. It is to seek an answer, an explanation. The disciples ask Jesus: 'Why do your disciples not follow the tradition?' (Mark 7:5), or the four disciples ask him this question: 'Tell us, when will these things happen?' (Mark 13:3). 2. To interrogate also means to examine someone with pointed questions, sometimes to test or put them to the test. The Pharisees interrogate Jesus about healing on the Sabbath (Matthew 12:10), not to learn, but to have something to accuse him of. Jesus himself questions his disciples: 'Who do people say that I am?' (Mark 8:27). 3. The word can also mean to ask, to plead, in the sense of soliciting someone insistently. This is the idea when one asks someone to do something (Matthew 16:1). 4. Finally, to ask a question can sometimes mean to challenge, to contest: 'They no longer dared to ask him any question' (Luke 20:40) means they abandoned their attempts to trap him.
G1905.origine: The word comes from the Greek root 'ἐρωτάω' (érōtaō), augmented by the prefix 'ἐπί' (épi) which reinforces the idea of direct action. The prefix 'ἐπί' suggests the idea of turning to someone, addressing them. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this verb mostly translates 'שׁאל' (shaʾal), which means to ask, and also 'דרשׁ' (darash), to seek or inquire. It is a common and active verb: to ask is to engage in an action directed towards someone to obtain a response.
G1905.emploi: This verb appears 56 times in the New Testament, very frequently in the first three Gospels, especially in Mark and Luke. It describes the interactions between Jesus and the crowds, the disciples, the adversaries. The disciples ask Jesus to understand his teachings or actions (Mark 9:32, Luke 2:46). The adversaries—Pharisees, Sadducees—interrogate him to test or trap him (Matthew 22:23-46, Mark 12:18-34). Jesus himself questions his disciples to make them think (Mark 8:27-29). The meaning sometimes shifts from 'to pose a question' to 'to ask insistently', as when one 'asks' the governor for the head of a prisoner (Matthew 27:58 involved in the context). The insistence of the verb (prefix 'ἐπί') emphasizes personal engagement: when one interrogates, one directly turns to someone, one addresses them.
G1905.portee: This verb reminds us that dialogue is at the heart of the Christian faith. Jesus does not impose his truths: he questions, he invites his disciples to ask, to seek an answer. The disciples freely interrogate, which shows that faith is not passive. For the reader, this word invites spiritual curiosity: it is legitimate to ask questions, to seek to understand the word of God. It is by asking Jesus and listening to his answers that the disciples and the crowds progress in knowledge.

sens: question or request addressed to someone
formal request or requirement
commitment or solemn promise to God
G1906.detail: 1. The word primarily means a question or request posed to someone: this is the basic idea of the Greek term. 2. It can refer to a more formal request or requirement, something that is claimed or demanded from someone. 3. In 1 Peter 3:21, it takes on a very specific meaning: the commitment of a good conscience toward God. Peter describes baptism not merely as a physical washing, but as an act by which the believer solemnly commits to God and expresses their faithfulness.
G1906.origine: The word comes from the Greek root erotao ("to ask"), preceded by the prefix epi ("upon," "toward"). It evokes the idea of posing a question or making a request to someone. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Aramaic word sheelah ("question"). The word family includes other terms denoting question or inquiry.
G1906.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 3:21. Peter uses it in a baptismal context that is rich in meaning: he explains that the believer's baptism is not valued by physical washing, but by the moral and spiritual commitment to God. It is a rare, almost technical term here, which emphasizes the solemn and personal nature of the promise made at the time of baptism.
G1906.portee: This word reminds the believer that baptism is not a mere rite or magical act, but a conscious step and a personal commitment to God. It is a call to sincerity and responsibility: entering into the Christian faith means binding oneself by a solemn promise, a "good conscience" before the Lord. This gives baptism all its depth: it is an act of will and heart, not just of the body.

sens: Keep something firmly in place
Present, offer, put forward
Direct attention toward, observe closely
Watch over, supervise
Remain, stay
G1907.detail: 1. In its primary sense, the verb means to hold or keep something firmly: it conveys the idea of retaining a grip, not letting go. 2. By extension, it means to present or offer something: one "holds" something in front of someone to give or show it to them. Thus, in Philippians 2:16, Paul speaks of "holding" or "bearing" the word of life, meaning to present it to the world. 3. The verb acquires the sense of observing or looking closely, particularly by directing one's mind toward something. In Acts 3:5, the beggar "looked intently" at Peter and John, focusing his attention on them in hopes of receiving something. 4. From this derives the sense of watching over, supervising, taking care: in 1 Timothy 4:16, Paul exhorts to "watch" oneself and one's teaching, meaning to maintain constant vigilance. 5. Finally, the verb can mean to remain or stay: in Acts 19:22, Paul "stayed" in Asia for some time longer, he remained there.
G1907.origine: The word is composed of the prefix ἐπί (epi, "upon") and the verb ἔχω (echō, "to have, to hold"). The basic image is thus one of "holding upon," that is, maintaining, retaining. This preposition ἐπί adds the idea of an action that pertains to something, that is exercised in its direction. In Hebrew, the verb χάδαλ (hadal, "to cease, to abstain") and other closely related forms are sometimes used in the same sense of restraint or vigilance.
G1907.emploi: The verb ἐπέχω appears 5 times in the New Testament. It carries several nuances depending on the context. In Acts 3:5, it expresses the sustained attention that the beggar gives to Peter and John. In Acts 19:22, it means to remain or stay in a place. In Philippians 2:16, it denotes the action of bearing or presenting the word of life. In 1 Timothy 4:16, it takes on the meaning of attentively watching over oneself and one's ministry. In Luke 14:7, used absolutely, it expresses careful observation. The context determines the exact nuance each time: attention, presentation, supervision, or staying.
G1907.portee: This verb highlights the biblical importance of attention and vigilance in the Christian life. Watching over oneself and one's teaching, as 1 Timothy 4:16 demands, is not merely an administrative recommendation: it is a spiritual posture, that of a heart that firmly holds onto the truth and holiness. Likewise, bearing the word of life means holding it before others as something infinitely precious. This word invites every believer to cultivate attentive vigilance in their faith.

sens: Harm someone through insulting words or actions
Insult, slander
Falsely accuse or speak ill of someone
G1908.detail:
1. To mistreat means to harm someone, particularly through hurtful words or acts of contempt. It is to treat someone harshly and with intent to harm. In Matthew 5:44 and Luke 6:28, Jesus asks his disciples to pray for those who mistreat them: this is a radical teaching, calling to love even those who do us harm.
2. The word also evokes direct insult, the slander spoken against someone. It is to speak ill of someone to their face or in their absence, with the intent to belittle them.
3. To mistreat can also refer to malicious accusation or slander: in 1 Peter 3:16, those who "slander" your good conduct seek to present you in a false light, to discredit you with deceptive words despite your innocence.
G1908.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of showing hostility or spite toward someone. The element "epi-" intensifies the action: to mistreat is to set oneself against someone with malice. It is a Greek word that describes an active form of contempt or verbal and behavioral hostility.
G1908.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament, always in ethical or persecution contexts. In Matthew 5:44 and Luke 6:28, Jesus uses it to describe what enemies or adversaries do to the disciples. In 1 Peter 3:16, the context is that of slander: people falsely accuse Christians of being wrongdoers, while they have good conduct. In all three cases, it is a hostile action motivated by malice, and in all cases, the Bible calls for not responding with the same hostility, but with blessing or integrity.
G1908.portee: Jesus teaches us that to be mistreated—receiving insults, false accusations, contempt—is part of the disciple's life, but our response must be love and prayer, not vengeance. This command reminds us that our worth is not in the opinion of others, but in our conscience before God and in our faithfulness to Christ. In the face of slander or disdain, the best defense is a righteous life and a loving response.

sens: placed or positioned above
toward a place, in the direction of
at the time of, during
because of, due to
against, in opposition to
concerning, regarding
G1909.detail:
1. **Placed or positioned above**: the most concrete and primary meaning of the word. It describes something that rests on a surface. For example, a seed sown "on" the ground (Mark 4:26), or Christ walking "on" the waters (Matthew 14:25). It is a spatial relationship of support or contact.

2. **Toward a place, in the direction of**: when it indicates movement. Jesus tells Peter to come "to" him on the waters (Matthew 14:28-29). This nuance shifts from rest to action, from "where?" to "where to go?".

3. **At the time of, during**: when it marks the moment. Matthew 1:11 states that Jeconiah was born "at" the time of the deportation to Babylon. The word situates an event within a historical period.

4. **Because of, due to**: it expresses the basis of an action or feeling. Romans 9:23 speaks of the riches of glory "toward" the vessels of mercy: mercy is the reason for this richness.

5. **Against, in opposition to**: it denotes hostility or conflict. Luke 12:52 speaks of family dissension: "three against two, two against three." The word shows confrontation.

6. **Concerning, regarding**: it introduces the theme of a word or thought. Acts 5:35 says to take heed "to" what you are about to do: it speaks *about* an action.
G1909.origine: The Greek word ἐπί comes from Indo-European and primarily expresses the idea of "superposition," of one thing placed "on" another. In classical Greek, it combines with three cases (genitive, dative, accusative) to refine this spatial idea into temporal, causal, or abstract ideas. The New Testament inherits this flexibility: the same small word adapts to very varied contexts, from the most concrete meaning (walking on water) to the most subtle meanings (the reason for a judgment). It is a very frequent word, fundamental for situating and connecting the elements of a narrative or argument.
G1909.emploi: The word ἐπί is one of the most used in the New Testament, with 792 occurrences. It appears in almost all books and takes on very diverse meanings depending on the context and grammatical case. With the genitive, it mainly indicates the place where one is or a historical period of time ("at the time of," Matthew 1:11). With the dative, it often expresses the reason, motive, or basis of an action (Romans 12:12, "rejoicing in hope"). With the accusative, the most frequent in the New Testament, it describes movement toward something or the descent of an action upon a person (Matthew 10:13, "peace be upon you"). Its meanings thus shift from spatial to temporal, from causal to directive, according to the needs of the text. It is a key word for understanding how events and thoughts are linked in biblical narration.
G1909.portee: This small word shows how God orders things in time and space. When the Holy Spirit descends "upon" the disciples (Acts 2:1-4), the word suggests a real and active presence. When Jesus speaks of building his Church "on" the rock (Matthew 16:18), the foundation becomes visible and solid. For the Christian reader, ἐπί reminds us that blessings and responsibilities are always "upon" us, concretely: it is not abstract, it is contact. Finally, this word helps to see how God's calls, the divisions of the world, and judgments are inscribed in real history.

sens: To get on or board an animal or vehicle
To board a boat
To head toward a place, to go there
To enter a region or space
G1910.detail:
1. To mount primarily means to climb onto the back of a beast of burden. It is the image of the king entering Jerusalem: "mounted on a donkey" (Matthew 21:5). The emphasis is on the physical act of positioning oneself on something or someone.
2. Boarding a boat, to mount means to embark, to cross the passage that separates the quay from the ship. Paul and his companions "went aboard a ship of Adramyttium" (Acts 27:2) to undertake their journey to Rome. It is always the movement of access to a means of transport.
3. To mount can also mean to head toward a place, to go there by physically ascending or advancing. "You know how, from the first day I entered Asia" (Acts 20:18): the verb describes Paul's arrival and presence in that region. Acts 25:1: Festus "arrived in the province" describes his accession to his position in that place.
4. Finally, to mount is used for the intention of going somewhere: "they told Paul not to go up to Jerusalem" (Acts 21:4). Here, the verb denotes the plan, the intended movement toward a destination.
G1910.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "epi" (on, against, toward) and the verb "baïnô" which means to walk, to go. Together, they form the idea of mounting, of placing oneself on something. The root evokes the concrete and physical action of climbing, of accessing height or advancing toward. In Hebrew, it is often the verb רָכַב (rakhab) that carries this meaning of riding or mounting.
G1910.emploi: This verb appears 6 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Acts of the Apostles (5 occurrences), and only once in Matthew. In Matthew 21:5, it describes the king riding on a donkey (quotation from Zechariah). In Acts, Paul and his companions board ships to travel (Acts 21:2 and 27:2). The verb is also used to express arrival and entry into a region: Paul "enters" Asia (Acts 20:18), Festus "arrives" in the province (Acts 25:1). Finally, it expresses the intention to go somewhere: not to "go up" to Jerusalem (Acts 21:4). The meaning varies according to the preposition that follows it (accusative for the object of the action, dative or "to" for the destination), but the central idea remains that of physical movement of access.
G1910.portee: This verb reminds us that the believer's life is a journey, a succession of movements, access to new places and new trials. Paul ascends toward Jerusalem knowing that the Spirit warns him of chains and suffering: it is a lesson in faith and obedience. The king who rides on a donkey teaches us the humility of the Messiah. For us, to mount also means to advance in faith, to accept the new challenges that God places on our path.

sens: Place or throw something on someone or something
Seize someone, stop or capture them
Rush or throw oneself on
Come to mind, occupy thought
Return or fall to someone's share
G1911.detail:
1. The basic meaning is physical: to place or set one thing upon another. One "puts" a piece of cloth on a garment (Matthew 9:16: "No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment"), or one "throws" clothes on an animal (Mark 11:7: the disciples "threw their garments" on the colt).

2. When one "puts a hand on" someone, it means to seize them, often to stop or capture them. Authorities seek to "put a hand" on Jesus (Luke 20:19), the apostles are arrested when a hand is "put" on them (Acts 5:18).

3. The verb can also express the action of rushing onto something with impetuosity: the waves crash onto the boat (Mark 4:37), or one puts a hand to the plow, meaning to engage in work (Luke 9:62).

4. Figuratively, "putting the mind on" means to focus attention on something, to think about it. Peter, thinking about his denial, "wept" (Mark 14:72).

5. In a context of sharing or inheritance, what "falls to someone's share" belongs to them or is their responsibility (Luke 15:12: the share that "falls to him").
G1911.origine: The Greek verb ἐπιβάλλω (epiballō) is composed of ἐπί (epi, "on") and βάλλω (ballō, "to throw, to cast"). Its primary image is that of throwing or placing something on a surface. In ancient Hebrew, it often translates the verbs שָׁלַח (šālaḥ, "to send, to throw") and שִׁית (šîth, "to place, to put"). This composition makes visible the close relationship between "placing" and "seizing": the one who throws their hands on someone seizes them.
G1911.emploi: This verb appears 18 times in the New Testament. It is used in all four gospels and in Acts, primarily in two contexts: first, the concrete actions of placing or throwing (fabrics, garments, hands), especially in Mark and Luke; secondly, arrest or capture (opponents seek to seize Jesus, Herod "begins" to persecute the Church). The verb also takes on a figurative nuance: thoughts that occupy the mind (Mark 14:72), and in a single passage (Luke 15:12), it takes on the meaning of what "falls to share." In Acts 12:1, "to begin to" marks the start of an action: Herod "began" to mistreat the believers.
G1911.portee: This word shows how the authorities and enemies of Jesus seek to "seize" him, but cannot succeed — the hand raised against him can only fall when his hour has come. It also reminds us of the importance of intention and the attention of the heart: "putting one's mind on" something means allowing it to occupy and transform us. Finally, it sheds light on the weight of the shares and responsibilities that "fall to us" in life.

sens: Impose a burden, a load on someone
Weigh on someone, be a burden or nuisance
Exaggerate, aggravate a matter
G1912.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of placing a weight, a burden on someone's shoulders — literally a physical load, but always in a figurative sense in the New Testament. It is to overwhelm someone with an obligation or expense.
2. "To be a burden" means to weigh on someone, to become a burden for them, particularly in terms of financial or material responsibility. Paul in 1 Thessalonians 2:9 and 2 Thessalonians 3:8 explains that he worked with his own hands "so as not to be a burden to any of you": he did not want the Church to have to feed or support him materially.
3. The verb can also mean to exaggerate or aggravate matters: in 2 Corinthians 2:5, Paul says "not to exaggerate anything" regarding a matter of punishment, meaning not to amplify its seriousness or importance beyond reality.
G1912.origine: The word combines the prefix ἐπι ("on") and βαρέω ("to load, to burden"), which comes from βάρος ("weight, burden"). The starting image is that of the weight placed on someone — hence the meaning of imposing a burden. This root is found in French in words like "barometer" (measure of air weight).
G1912.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the New Testament, all in Paul. In 1 Thessalonians 2:9 and 2 Thessalonians 3:8, Paul uses it to describe his refusal to become a financial burden to the churches: he works hard night and day to remain self-sufficient and not weigh on them. This practice reveals his love for the Thessalonians and his apostolic independence. In 2 Corinthians 2:5, the same verb means rather to exaggerate or amplify: Paul asserts that he does not want to aggravate the judgment concerning the one who has caused sorrow.
G1912.portee: This word shows how aware Paul was of the material burden that a teacher can represent for a poor church, and how he deliberately chose to work to lighten that burden. For the Christian today, it teaches the importance of financial independence in service and respect for others' resources. It is also a reminder that our words and actions can "load" or burden others — hence the importance of measure and accuracy.

sens: Put someone on the back of a saddle animal
Make someone mount a beast of burden
Lead someone by taking them on an animal
G1913.detail:
1. The word describes the concrete action of placing a person on the back of a beast of burden (donkey, horse, mule) for transport. The Good Samaritan in Luke 10:34 "put" the wounded traveler on his own mount to take him to the inn. It is a gesture of practical help: the beast becomes the means of transport for the passenger.
2. It can also evoke the action of making someone mount, as when they "made Jesus mount" the colt in Luke 19:35 after throwing their garments on its back. Here the meaning shifts towards the idea of "saddling up."
3. The word can finally mean "to lead" in the sense of "to conduct by transporting": in Acts 23:24, the soldiers must "lead" Paul safely to the governor with mounts provided for him. It is less the punctual action of placing him than the idea of transporting him from one place to another.
G1913.origine: The word combines the prefix "epi" (on, above) and "bibazō" (to place, to make go). The root "bebēka" or "bebēka" evokes movement and walking. In Hebrew, it primarily translates the verb "rākab" and its derivatives (to make mount, to saddle), hence the image of a person placed on a beast of burden. The preposition "epi" reinforces the idea of placement "on" the mount.
G1913.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, always in Luke, who uses it to describe concrete acts of transport. In Luke 10:34, it is the gesture of charity of the Samaritan who cares for and transports the wounded. In Luke 19:35, it is the preparation of the procession of Jesus entering Jerusalem. In Acts 23:24, it is the order of the Roman commander to escort Paul on horseback to the governor. The context varies (charity, royal welcome, administrative security), but the meaning remains material: to physically place someone on a beast of burden to move them.
G1913.portee: This humble word reminds us that in the biblical world, saddle animals are instruments of help and dignity. The Good Samaritan "mounts" the wounded man on his mount — it is an act of practical and costly tenderness. For the reader, this verb makes concrete the care for one's neighbor and emphasizes that God's love is expressed through tangible, visible, and sometimes disruptive gestures.

sens: Plan secret pour piéger ou tuer quelqu'un
Piège tendu contre une personne
Projet de mal contre autrui
G1917.detail: 1. The word ambush refers to a secret plan, a conspiracy plotted against someone to harm them, take their life, or capture them. In Acts 9:24, after his conversion, Saul is threatened by a plot from the Jews who want to kill him, and they guard the city gates day and night to capture him. 2. It evokes the idea of a trap or a setup: one lays an ambush as one lays a net. In Acts 20:3, the Jews "set ambushes" for Paul, meaning they secretly organize an attack against him during his travels. 3. The word emphasizes the malicious and organized nature of the plan: it is not mere hostility, but a carefully thought-out and concerted plan among several people to do harm. In Acts 23:30, the Roman commander reports that they were "laying ambushes" for Paul and that he must be kept safe by being handed over to the governor.
G1917.origine: The Greek word ἐπιβουλή is composed of ἐπί ("against") and βουλή ("counsel, deliberation, plan"). It literally designates a plan formed against someone. The root evokes the idea of a concerted will, of a secret deliberation: people gather to plan evil. It is a classical Greek formation, very natural and expressive, with no direct link to the Hebrew of the Old Testament, but it conveys well the sense of organized threat.
G1917.emploi: The word ambush appears 4 times in Acts, all related to threats against Paul: after his conversion (9:24), during his journey in Greece (20:3), in his testimony to the governor (20:19), and in the report of the Roman commander (23:30). Each time, it involves concerted plans by the Jews to arrest or kill the apostle. The context shows that these ambushes are serious and very real: they justify security measures (guards at the gates, transport by Roman force). Paul faces them in his apostolic ministry and missionary journeys.
G1917.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that following Christ does not spare one from the attacks and plots of the adversaries of the Gospel. Paul knows the ambushes, but they do not stop him: he continues his mission. It is a lesson in perseverance in faith despite danger, and an invitation to trust in God in the face of visible and hidden obstacles in the world.

sens: To unite in marriage with the widow of a deceased close relative, according to the custom of levirate
To fulfill the legal obligation to perpetuate the name of a deceased person by marrying his widow
G1918.detail:
1. The levirate was a custom of the people of Israel: when a man died without children, his brother or a close relative was obligated to marry his widow to provide children for the deceased and perpetuate his name. In Matthew 22:24, the Sadducees describe this practice by saying: "Teacher, Moses said: If a man dies without children, his brother shall marry his wife and raise up offspring for his brother."

2. The word refers to the act of entering into this replacement marital relationship. It is a commitment to the family of the deceased as much as to the widow, for the child born would be legally counted as that of the first husband. This obligation was taken seriously in ancient Israel, even though not everyone adhered to it (see the story of Judah and Tamar in Genesis 38).
G1918.origine: The Greek word combines the prefix "epi" (upon, towards) and the noun "gambros" (relative by marriage, brother-in-law). It literally describes the action of "becoming a relative by marriage" or "entering into a relationship of kinship through marriage." This word translates the Hebrew "yabam" (Genesis 38:8), which refers to the levirate law mentioned in Deuteronomy 25:5-10. The word expresses a very ancient legal and familial obligation.
G1918.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 22:24, in a question that the Sadducees pose to Jesus to test him. They describe the levirate as a command of Moses in order to create a logical contradiction: if seven brothers successively married the same woman according to this law, to whom would she belong at the resurrection? Jesus responds by showing that the Sadducees are ignorant of the power of God and the Scriptures. The context shows that this practice, although ancient and mentioned in the Law, was primarily known through first-century Jewish theology.
G1918.portee: This word reminds Christians that the Law of Israel contained human and concrete rules to protect widows and preserve families. Encountering it helps us better understand the Sadducees' question and Jesus' answer about the resurrection: Jesus asserts that God is not the God of the dead, but of the living, which transcends human categories of earthly marriage. It is an invitation to distinguish between earthly practices and eternal realities.

sens: Belonging to the earth, to the visible physical world
Concerning what is material, carnal, opposed to the spiritual
Limited to the present time, temporal
G1919.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what belongs to the earth or to this visible and physical world, in contrast to the heavens. In 1 Corinthians 15:40, Paul contrasts "earthly bodies" with "heavenly bodies": the former are those we know on earth, the latter are those of the resurrection. In Philippians 2:10, "the earth" simply refers to the earthly domain where we live, at the horizontal level of creation.

2. Subsequently, the word takes on a moral charge: it describes what is carnal, material in the sense of carnal desires and purely selfish concerns. In Philippians 3:19, those who "set their minds on earthly things" only pursue their carnal passions and their belly. In James 3:15, "earthly wisdom" is that which arises from fleshly desires and opposes the heavenly wisdom that comes from God.

3. Finally, the word characterizes what belongs to the present time, the temporal order. In 2 Corinthians 5:1, our "earthly dwelling" — this tent, our current body — is temporary and destined to be replaced by an "eternal dwelling" in heaven. John 3:12 contrasts the "earthly things" that the disciples can observe with the "heavenly things" that pertain to divine revelation.
G1919.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: ἐπί (epi, "upon") and γῆ (gè, "earth"). It literally means "that which is upon the earth." In Hebrew, the idea is found with words like ארץ (eretz, "earth"). It is a descriptive word, simply formed in Greek to express belonging to the earthly or material domain, without an initial pejorative nuance — the context gives the word its positive or negative coloring.
G1919.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and in the epistle of James. Three meanings intertwine: first, simple geography or physicality (1 Corinthians 15:40 on bodies, 2 Corinthians 5:1 on the tent of the body), then the morality of carnal desire (Philippians 3:19, James 3:15), and finally the opposition between the temporal and the eternal (John 3:12, 2 Corinthians 5:1). The word does not automatically condemn the earth or the body, but emphasizes that what is merely earthly is unstable, limited, and, if it absorbs all human desire, distant from God.
G1919.portee: This word reminds Christians that there are two orders: the earthly and the heavenly. It is not about despising the body or creation, but about refusing to idolize them or confine our thoughts to them. Jesus invites his disciples to also embrace the "heavenly things" — the revelation of God. The Christian must keep their eyes lifted toward the eternal, without denying the present, but without giving it the final word.

sens: To manifest, appear suddenly (for a meteorological phenomenon)
To arrive, occur unexpectedly
G1920.detail:
1. The word describes the sudden appearance of a natural phenomenon, particularly of the wind. In Acts 28:13, Paul and his companions are at sea: "the south wind blew up the next day" means that the wind began to blow, creating the conditions for the boat to move forward. It is the image of the wind that surges, that is born.

2. More broadly, the verb expresses the idea of something that happens, that occurs — whether it be an event, a circumstance, or a force of nature. The word suggests an appearance that imposes itself, often without having been seen coming.
G1920.origine: The word combines two elements: "epi" (upon, above) and "ginomai" (to become, to be born, to occur). The basic image is thus that of something that "becomes" or "occurs" at the surface, that surges. It is the same simple verb "ginomai" that also simply expresses "to happen" or "to take place" in the New Testament.
G1920.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 28:13, in the account of Paul's journey to Rome. Here, it refers to the south wind that suddenly rises and allows the ship to advance. The use in ancient Greek texts outside the Bible (notably in the Letter of Jeremiah) shows that the verb applies to events or phenomena that occur, that happen at a given moment. The maritime context emphasizes the aspect of a sudden and useful appearance.
G1920.portee: This word reminds us that Paul, on his way to Rome to face his trial, depended on natural conditions — the wind, the currents, the seasons. It is a concrete trace of his humanity and his trust in God amid unpredictable circumstances. The wind that rises is also God acting through the ordinary means of creation to pursue His purpose.

sens: Perceive, discern through the senses or intelligence
Identify someone among others
Discover, learn, ascertain a fact
Know intimately or personally
Distinguish, discern good from evil
G1921.detail:
1. To perceive or discern something through careful observation: it is to see clearly what is happening within oneself or around oneself. Jesus "immediately knew in himself that power had gone out from him" (Mark 5:30) — he perceived inwardly what had just occurred.
2. To identify a person, to recognize them among others: it is to know who they are when you see them. The disciples "did not recognize him" on the road to Emmaus, then "recognized him" at the breaking of the bread (Luke 24:16, 31).
3. To discover or learn a fact through inquiry, reflection, or narrative: it is to move from ignorance to certainty. A sinful woman "having learned that he was at table," heard this news and came (Luke 7:37).
4. To know someone intimately, in a deep personal relationship: it is much more than simply knowing who they are. Saint Paul says, "I will know as I have been known" (1 Corinthians 13:12) — a mutual and complete knowledge, face to face.
5. To distinguish good from evil, to recognize moral quality: "You will recognize them by their fruits" (Matthew 7:16) — to identify the true nature by its manifestations.
G1921.origine: This word comes from the simple verb γινώσκω ("to know, to understand"), augmented by the prefix ἐπι ("upon, towards"). It expresses a more active and directed knowledge, a recognition that goes towards something or someone. Thus, it is a synonym of the simple verb, but marked by the idea of discernment, identification, or discovery. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates notably the Hebrew verb נָכַר ("to recognize, to distinguish").
G1921.emploi: This verb appears about forty times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. It can be constructed in several ways: absolute (simply "to recognize," "to know"), with a direct object (what is recognized or learned), or with a conjunction introducing what is discovered. It primarily describes sensory or spiritual perception (perceiving a power going out from someone, Mark 5:30), visual identification of people (recognizing a man, Luke 24:31), learning of news (Luke 7:37), inquiry by authorities to discover facts (Acts 9:30, 24:8), and finally the intimate knowledge face to face promised to the redeemed (1 Corinthians 13:12). The word emphasizes less simple knowledge than the active process of discernment and recognition.
G1921.portee: This verb shows us that true knowledge is an act of discernment and identification, not passive information. In faith, "to recognize" is to truly see who Jesus is, to discern the fruits of the Spirit, to learn the depths of God. For the Christian, there is a double call: until then, we recognize "in part"; but we will walk towards this intimate knowledge, face to face, that awaits us eternally with the Lord.

sens: Acquaintance or familiarity with someone or something
Clear discernment, clear recognition of a reality
Practical and living knowledge, not theoretical but internal and transformative
Knowledge of God in particular, the fruit of revelation and personal relationship
Knowledge of the truth of the Gospel
Knowledge of Christ in his fullness and saving effectiveness
G1922.detail:
1. It is primarily to know something clearly and precisely, to recognize it without confusion. The word suggests an acquaintance, a familiarity based on a true encounter.

2. This knowledge is not vague: it is a discernment, an ability to see rightly and truly understand what is. Romans 1:28 speaks of those who "did not care to know God" — it is to refuse this clear and precise knowledge.

3. What distinguishes this word is that it denotes a living knowledge that transforms. In Colossians 3:10, the believer "is renewed in knowledge" — this knowledge renews the whole person, not just the mind.

4. Often, this knowledge pertains to God himself. Ephesians 1:17 prays that believers receive it; it then comes from spiritual revelation, not from human effort.

5. It also concerns "the truth" of the Gospel. In 2 Timothy 3:7, false teachers "are always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth" — they remain always on the surface, without penetrating the heart of salvation.

6. Finally, it can designate a personal communion with the risen Christ (2 Peter 1:2-3), where knowledge and relationship intertwine together.
G1922.origine: The word comes from the verb "epigignôskô" (to recognize, to truly know) formed from the prefix "epi" (above, in addition) and "gignôskô" (to know, to recognize). This prefix reinforces the idea: a knowledge that goes to the end, that penetrates, that adds to an initial apprehension. In the Greek Old Testament, it renders the Hebrew "daat" (knowledge, understanding), notably in Proverbs 2:5 and Hosea 4:1 where it denotes a true relationship with God, not a dead knowledge.
G1922.emploi: This word appears 20 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Pauline epistles and 2 Peter. Paul uses it to describe the knowledge of God and his will, asking that believers be "filled" with it (Colossians 1:9). It also designates the knowledge of the truth of the Gospel: it is to this that the false teachers of 2 Timothy 3:7 never truly access. In Hebrews 10:26, sinning "after receiving the knowledge of the truth" aggravates judgment — this knowledge entails responsibility. 2 Peter emphasizes the knowledge of Christ as the source of spiritual strength and grace. The word always implies a complete, precise, transformative knowledge, far beyond mere information.
G1922.portee: This knowledge is not reserved for scholars: it is the right and calling of every Christian to truly know God and his Son personally, in a way that brings renewal and change. It comes from revelation and the Holy Spirit, not from human effort alone. It also carries a responsibility: knowing the truth requires submission to it and living by it.

sens: Text engraved or written on an object
Written formula displayed officially or publicly
G1923.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a text engraved or written on a material object — such as on a coin. When Jesus asks his disciples to show him the coin for the tax, he asks them: "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" (Matthew 22:20) — he speaks of the name of Caesar inscribed on the coin.
2. The word takes on a broader and more official meaning: an inscription can be a sign, a poster, a text displayed publicly for a serious reason. Thus, above the cross of Jesus was written the inscription: "This is the King of the Jews" (Luke 23:38). Mark specifies that this inscription indicated "the charge against him" (Mark 15:26) — it was the official accusation publicly displayed.
G1923.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to write upon," formed from "upon" and "to write." It is a simple and common word in Greek: it describes the action of inscribing something on a durable surface — stone, metal, wood — so that the message lasts and is visible to all.
G1923.emploi: The word appears only 5 times in the New Testament, always in the Gospels. It returns twice regarding the coin with Caesar's likeness: in Matthew 22:20 and Mark 12:16, during the debate about the tribute. The other three uses concern the inscription on the cross: Mark 15:26 describes it as the official announcement of the condemnation, while Luke 20:24 briefly mentions it in the same scene with the coin, and Luke 23:38 reports the exact text displayed above Jesus. In all cases, it refers to words engraved or written in a durable, visible, and official manner.
G1923.portee: The inscription on the cross reveals with impressive sobriety what was at stake: Jesus was executed for having been proclaimed — and having proclaimed himself — king. This title "The King of the Jews," displayed for all to see, summarizes the scandal and the truth of his passion. For the believer, this word reminds us that faith does not rest on erased words, but on publicly attested facts.

sens: To trace characters or words on a visible surface
To inscribe a text, a name, or a formula in a lasting manner
To engrave something in a heart or conscience in an indelible way
G1924.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to write on something: to trace letters or words on a surface, as one writes an inscription. At Calvary, Pontius Pilate had the accusation written on the cross: "Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews" (Mark 15:26). The Athenians had inscribed on an altar the words "To an unknown god" (Acts 17:23).
2. The word also denotes the action of engraving or inscribing durably, which creates a visible and permanent trace. The names of the twelve tribes of Israel were inscribed on the twelve gates of the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:12).
3. In a figurative sense, it means to place something in the heart or mind in an indelible way, as if engraving letters there. God promises to write His laws in the hearts of His people, which means to place them intimately and permanently, not on tablets of stone (Hebrews 8:10; 10:16).
G1924.origine: The word comes from the Greek root "graphô" (to write) preceded by the prefix "epi" (on). The basic image is that of an act of writing that takes place on a surface: to inscribe, mark, engrave. In Hebrew, the underlying word "katab" has the same concrete meaning of writing on something. The prefix "epi" specifies that the writing is done not in a void, but on an object, a substance, a heart.
G1924.emploi: The verb appears five times in the New Testament, only in the later Gospels and the epistles. Three usages are concrete: the inscription of the condemnation on the cross (Mark 15:26), the inscription on the Athenian altar (Acts 17:23), and the names engraved on the gates of the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:12). Two usages are figurative and theological: in Hebrews 8:10 and 10:16, which quote the prophecy of Jeremiah, God commits to writing His law not on external tablets, but in the heart and mind of the renewed people. This image transforms writing into a symbol of an inner and living covenant.
G1924.portee: This word reminds Christians that God desires to write His will not only externally, but deep within us. The Gospel operates a transition from the Law engraved on stone to the Law written in the heart — an inner and personal transformation. It is a strong image of the new birth and sanctification: our hearts become like living tablets where God engraves His love and will.

sens: To present something to the view, to exhibit it
To make someone see by guiding or sending them somewhere
To demonstrate, to prove by reasoning or evidence
To display, to highlight publicly
G1925.detail:
1. To show means to present something to someone's eyes for them to see. When the Pharisees ask Jesus to "show" them a sign from heaven (Matthew 16:1), they want Him to display His power. When the disciples "point out" to Jesus the buildings of the temple, they are showing them to Him, making them visible (Matthew 24:1).
2. The verb also means to send someone to show something or to appear somewhere. Jesus tells the lepers: "Go show yourselves to the priests" — that is, go present yourselves to them so they can confirm your healing (Luke 17:14).
3. To show also means to demonstrate, to prove something by arguing or providing evidence. Apollos "refutes the Jews publicly, demonstrating by the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ" — he proves by the text that Jesus is the Messiah (Acts 18:28).
4. The word carries the idea of making something evident, making it publicly visible. God wants to "show" the immutability of His promise with more "evidence" by committing Himself with an oath (Hebrews 6:17) — He makes His commitment irrevocable for all to see.
G1925.origine: The word comes from two parts: "epi" (upon, over) and "deiknumi" (to show, to make visible). The image is that of pointing to something, designating it with a finger. In Greek, this verb retains this basic meaning: to make known by sight. The simple verb "deiknumi" simply means to show; the prefix "epi" emphasizes the action, making it more direct or public.
G1925.emploi: This verb appears 7 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Acts. Matthew uses it twice to describe how people ask Jesus to show or make visible (16:1; 22:19; 24:1). Luke uses it for the account of the healed lepers that Jesus sends to show themselves to the priests (17:14). Acts features it with Peter seeing the garments of Dorcas (9:39) and with Apollos proving that Jesus is the Christ (18:28). Hebrews uses it to affirm that God wants to show with evidence the immutability of His oath (6:17). The verb oscillates between simple exhibition and logical demonstration.
G1925.portee: This verb reminds us that in the New Testament, faith in Jesus does not rest on secrecy, but on what is shown, exhibited, made visible, and demonstrable. Jesus highlights His acts and signs; Apollos argues from Scripture; God supports His promise with an oath. For the reader, it is a lesson: Christian truth relies on facts that can be shown and arguments that can be presented.

sens: To accept someone, to welcome them
To greet with hospitality
To admit, to allow
G1926.detail:
1. To accept someone as welcome means to recognize and consent to their arrival. In 3 John 1:9, Diotrephes refuses to receive the apostle John — he does not welcome him, he rejects him.
2. To receive with hospitality means to give a warm welcome, food, and lodging, as one should to a brother or a traveler. In 3 John 1:10, Diotrephes refuses both to receive the brothers and to allow others to do so: this is a failure of Christian hospitality.
3. More broadly, the word can also refer to the acceptance or admission of something, the capacity to tolerate or allow it, although this meaning is less visible in biblical usages.
G1926.origine: The Greek word combines the prefix "epi" (upon, above) and the verb "dechomai" (to receive, to welcome). This composition emphasizes the idea of receiving someone close to oneself, admitting them into one's space or circle. In classical and later Greek, the verb also appears to mean "to accept" in a broader sense, particularly the conditions of an agreement.
G1926.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in 3 John, the shortest epistle of the New Testament. It deals with a conflict of hospitality: John rebukes Diotrephes for refusing to receive the brothers and even preventing others from being received. The context shows that "to receive" does not merely mean to politely recognize someone, but to concretely welcome them, with actions — sharing the table, the home, the friendship — which was a vital issue for missionaries and itinerant preachers in the first century.
G1926.portee: This word reminds the reader of a central virtue of Christian life: hospitality, an expression of practical love towards brothers and travelers. By refusing to receive, Diotrephes commits a double sin — pride and lack of charity. For every believer, the welcome offered or refused reflects the echo of the heart towards Jesus Himself (Matthew 25:35).

sens: To be present in a place, to inhabit it
To stay temporarily somewhere
To spend time in a place
G1927.detail:
1. To be present in a place, to inhabit it: the word simply describes the fact of being there, residing, or occupying a space. In Acts 2:10, it refers to Jews "dwelling in Jerusalem" — people who live there or are present.
2. To stay temporarily somewhere: this means to inhabit a place for a time, without necessarily being established there permanently. The sense focuses on presence, whether long or short.
3. To spend time in a place: in Acts 17:21, the Athenians "dwelling" in Athens spent their time discussing news — the verb emphasizes that they were occupied there, that they were staying.
G1927.origine: The word comes from the Greek δῆμος (dêmos: the people, the community of a city) and the prefix ἐπι (épi: on, towards). The basic image is therefore "to be at home among the people" or "to be present in the city." It is a common word in classical Greek (Plato, Xenophon) to denote the act of dwelling or staying somewhere.
G1927.emploi: This verb appears twice in the New Testament, in Acts. In Acts 2:10, it refers to the Jews "dwelling" in Jerusalem — those who lived or stayed in the holy city. In Acts 17:21, it describes the Athenians and foreigners who spent their time in Athens, busy discussing. In both cases, the word simply emphasizes the fact of being present in a place, without particular connotation. It is an ordinary verb that expresses residence or temporary presence without theological nuance.
G1927.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian message is addressed to people rooted in specific places — cities, communities. The witnesses who heard Peter and Paul lived, dwelled in Jerusalem and Athens. The presence of the Holy Spirit and the proclamation of the Gospel do not occur in the abstract, but at the heart of these concrete geographical and social realities.

sens: To add a clause or provision to a legal document after its initial drafting
To modify or complete a written commitment by inserting new stipulations
G1928.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of adding clauses or provisions to a legal document — contract, will, agreement — after its initial drafting. It is a legal act that modifies the original text by inserting new content. Paul uses it in Galatians 3:15: a well-established provision made by a man (a contract or a will) cannot be annulled or modified by anyone — no one can "add" new conditions once it is validated.
2. More broadly, the word evokes the idea of completing or modifying a written commitment. In the context of ancient judicial practice, it is an act reserved for one who has the authority to do so: one cannot add to a document that has already taken effect without the agreement of all parties or the competent authority.
G1928.origine: The word is composed of the preposition "epi" (on, above, towards) and the verb "diatassō" (to order, to arrange). This composition suggests the idea of arranging in addition, of adding on top. The verb is used in ancient Greek legal and administrative language for official acts — wills, contracts, edicts — where precision of terms was crucial.
G1928.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 3:15. Paul uses it in a legal reasoning: he compares the law of Moses to a valid and irrevocable testamentary provision. Just as no one can add to a properly established will once it is made, so the promise made to Abraham could not be annulled or modified by the law given four hundred thirty years later. It is a common legal argument that Greek-speaking readers would have understood immediately.
G1928.portee: This word reminds Christians that God's commitments are inviolable and definitive. God's promise to Abraham was not revoked or altered by the law; it remains valid. This passage sheds light on the permanence of divine grace and the irrevocable nature of the covenant with God's people — a foundational truth for Christian freedom in the face of legal demands.

sens: To hand something to someone
To present, to offer
To yield, to relinquish
G1929.detail:
1. To hand something to someone: this is the act of giving an object by passing it from one's hands to those of another person. Jesus uses it when he speaks of a father who gives bread to his son (Matthew 7:9), or when the book of Isaiah is handed to Jesus in the synagogue (Luke 4:17). It is a concrete gesture, a direct exchange.
2. To present or offer: sometimes it is less about passing from hand to hand than the act of extending, delivering something to someone for them to use or receive. At the table, Jesus breaks the bread and gives it to his disciples (Luke 24:30): he presents it to them for them to eat. It is a generous or ritual act.
3. To yield, to relinquish: in Acts 27:15, the ship "gave way" to the winds, meaning it yielded, it abandoned all resistance to the storm. The verb expresses here letting go, no longer holding back.
G1929.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "epi" (towards, on) and "didômi" (to give), which comes from an ancient root expressing the action of handing over. In Greek, related words like "didômi" or "dosis" (gift) share the same root. This composition "epi-didômi" adds the idea of a direct handing over, a transmission from hand to hand towards someone. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb "natan" (נתן), which means "to give."
G1929.emploi: This verb appears 9 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. Luke and Matthew use it in the parable of the Father and the child (Matthew 7:9-10; Luke 11:11-12), where Jesus asks: what father would give a stone to his son if he asks for bread? It is a logical appeal to the goodness of parents. Luke also uses it for the handing over of the book to Jesus (4:17) and the sharing of bread at the table (24:30, 42), where the verb emphasizes the liturgical or fraternal gesture of transmission. In Acts 27:15, the only usage without a direct object, it describes the ship yielding to the winds. The verb remains simple and direct, without moral or theological nuance: it is to give in the most natural sense.
G1929.portee: This word reminds us that giving is a fundamental gesture of love. Jesus uses it to show us how an earthly father gives good things to his child, so that we understand the generosity of the Heavenly Father (Matthew 7:9-11). At the table, this same verb describes the handing over of bread in intimacy, suggesting that giving and sharing create communion. It is a word that invites every Christian to imitate this generosity towards others.

sens: Arrange, organize what is disordered or incomplete
Establish, regulate in a methodical and lasting way
G1930.detail:
1. The verb evokes the action of arranging, organizing, putting in order what lacks structure or completeness. Paul says to Titus: "you set in order what remains to be arranged" (Titus 1:5), meaning to correct deficiencies, to fill gaps in the organization of the church in Crete.
2. More broadly, it is to establish things in a stable and lasting way, according to a thoughtful plan. In Crete, it involves putting in place a true ecclesiastical structure: appointing elders in every city, providing clear rules. It is a work of correction and structuring that goes beyond mere repair.
G1930.origine: The Greek word combines three elements: "epi" (upon, beyond, complement), "dia" (through), and "orthóō" (to set right, to straighten). The image is one of straightening what is crooked, correcting deeply. It is an enhancement of the simple verb "orthóō", a correction or arrangement that goes beyond the strict necessary, a perfection. The Pauline context suggests an ecclesiastical setting in good order.
G1930.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 1:5. Paul uses it to describe Titus's mission in Crete: "set in order what remains to be arranged". The context shows that it involves correcting the shortcomings of the church's organization, particularly by appointing elders (bishops, presbyters) in every city. Thus, it is a technical term, Pauline, to designate the organization and consolidation of the pastoral structure of a nascent ecclesial community.
G1930.portee: This word reminds the Christian that order in the church is not superficial: it is a pastoral and spiritual act, a desire for consolidation and durability. For a leader, it evokes the duty not to leave the work unfinished, but to "arrange" the deficiencies, to structure solidly. It is also an invitation to recognize that ecclesial edification requires work, method, and gentle firmness.

sens: To go down below the horizon, speaking of the sun
To come to an end, to disappear
G1931.detail:
1. The word literally refers to the setting of the sun, its movement of descending below the horizon at the end of the day. It is the natural image of the daily cycle: the sun "sets" when night arrives (Ephesians 4:26).
2. Figuratively, it describes anything that comes to an end or disappears: an anger that "sets" upon someone, is an anger that rests upon them, lasts, remains like the sun that persists until it has set. Paul uses this image to say: do not let your anger settle and take root in you until evening.
G1931.origine: The Greek word combines the prefix "epi" (upon, towards) and "dûô" (to plunge, to descend). It is the same verb that describes the setting of the sun in Hebrew ("bô'" in the Greek passages of the Old Testament cited: Deuteronomy 24:15, Joshua 8:29, Jeremiah 15:9). The image is one of a downward movement, an immersion beneath the horizon.
G1931.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 4:26, where Paul takes up a counsel from Psalm 4:5 to regulate the anger of Believers. In this context, "do not let the sun set on your anger" is a poetic and concrete image: it invites the believer to resolve their conflict before nightfall, before anger settles in permanently. The verb, common in Greek to describe the setting of the sun, becomes here a metaphor for calming and reconciliation.
G1931.portee: This biblical image invites the Christian not to let anger take root in them, but to resolve it quickly, while there is still time. It teaches that anger, like the passing day, must have an end: to pass without leaving a lasting trace. It is a call to prompt reconciliation and humility in fraternal relationships.

sens: The quality of one who is just and measured in judgment, without excess or harshness
The benevolent sweetness of a person towards another
The ability to be fair and reasonable in a difficult situation
G1932.detail:
1. Goodness first denotes a natural equity, a justness of judgment that does not confine itself to the strict application of rules. It is the quality of one who looks at things with a right and just gaze, capable of seeing beyond the letter. When Paul speaks of the "goodness" of Christ (2 Corinthians 10:1), he evokes this disposition to be just while remaining tender.
2. It is also the benevolent sweetness, tenderness in relationships. This goodness manifests as a strength of one who could act harshly but chooses indulgence and understanding. It is not weakness, but restrained strength with kindness.
3. Finally, it expresses reasonableness, this disposition to be fair when one has power over someone. As in Acts 24:4, where the lawyer Tertullus asks Governor Felix to listen "in your goodness", he requests the gentle exercise of just authority.
G1932.origine: This Greek word comes from the adjective ἐπιεικής (epieikès), which literally means "turned towards" (ἐπί, towards) "what is fitting" (εἰκός, what is appropriate). The image is that of someone whose judgment leans towards equity and reason, rather than clinging to the bare rule. This quality always seeks what is just and humane in a particular case.
G1932.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Acts 24:4, Tertullus, the prosecutor's lawyer, addresses the Roman governor Felix, asking him to listen with goodness: it is a polite request to one who holds authority, inviting him to exercise his power with equity and humanity. In 2 Corinthians 10:1, Paul speaks of "the gentleness and goodness of Christ": he associates here two complementary qualities, Christ being presented as one who judges with justice and kindness. This rarity makes these two uses all the more significant: it is a virtue that Paul and the early Christians saw as essential in a leader and in Christ.
G1932.portee: This goodness reminds us that true justice is never cold or rigid. It is mixed with mercy and understanding of the particular case. For the believer, recognizing the goodness of Christ means accepting that His judgment upon us is not a mere mechanical application of the law, but a just and tender gaze. It also invites us to cultivate this same quality in our relationships with others: to exercise authority, correction, or judgment with equity and gentleness rather than harshness.

sens: quality of being easy to live with, kind and moderate in judgments
equity, justice tempered by gentleness rather than by the strictness of the law
absence of harshness or violence in tone and gestures
G1933.detail: 1. Gentleness is a fundamental moral quality: it is the disposition of one who treats others with kindness and without excessive harshness. In Philippians 4:5, the apostle exhorts believers to let their gentleness "be known to all men," meaning to demonstrate it concretely in their relationships. 2. It is also a form of practical equity: not applying the law blindly, but adapting it with justice and compassion to specific situations. James 3:17 lists the wisdom from above as "gentle" (this word), peaceable, and full of mercy — a justice that knows how to yield and forgive. 3. Finally, it stands in opposition to violence and harshness of character. In 1 Peter 2:18, servants must be obedient even "to those who are difficult in character" — the opposite of gentleness. In 1 Timothy 3:3, a church leader must not be violent, but "gentle," able to exercise restraint.
G1933.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and literally denotes what is "suitable" or "appropriate" (from the verb "to seem, to appear"). It has specialized to describe the virtue of one who knows how to adapt their conduct to reality, who does not confine themselves to rigidity. It is the moral quality of one who tempers justice with equity: not a lack of principle, but a practical wisdom that knows when to be firm and when to be lenient.
G1933.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the New Testament, always to describe a moral quality expected of Christians. In the pastoral epistles (1 Timothy 3:3 and Titus 3:2), it is required of leaders and believers in general: to be gentle, not violent or excessive in judgment. In 1 Peter 2:18, it characterizes the conduct of the servant in the face of a difficult master — the virtue of not retaliating with harshness. James 3:17 places it among the fruits of true wisdom, alongside purity and mercy. Philippians 4:5 calls it "gentleness" and asks that it be visible, known, manifest — a virtue that should shine outwardly.
G1933.portee: This virtue invites the Christian to go beyond mere legal justice and to cultivate an active kindness, capable of adapting the application of principles to concrete situations. It teaches that moral strength lies not in rigidity or violence, but in the ability to be just while remaining human and merciful. For the one who practices it, it creates peace; for the one who receives it, it brings relief and hope.

sens: To look for something insistently, actively pursuing it
To ask, demand, have a desire for something
To seek to obtain, aspire to
To inquire, ask someone
G1934.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is to seek something with marked intention, often by pursuing it: it is to actively seek, not just to look around. Matthew 6:32 speaks of the pagans who "seek" food and clothing — they seek them relentlessly, as these things constantly preoccupy them.

2. The word also expresses the idea of asking or demanding something: to have a desire, to express a wish. In Acts 13:7, the proconsul shows the "desire" to hear the word of God — he expresses the wish, he makes the request.

3. To seek can mean to aspire to something, to deeply desire it as a future goal or ideal. In Hebrews 11:14, the patriarchs "seek" a heavenly homeland — they aim for it, making it their goal, not just out of curiosity but from conviction of the heart.

4. Finally, the word can mean to inquire of someone, to ask questions to obtain an answer or information, such as seeking to know someone's intentions or plans.
G1934.origine: The Greek word combines the prefix "epi" (which indicates direction, a particular intention) and "zêtéô" (to seek). This gives "epizêtéô" a more marked nuance: it is not a simple vague search, but a directed, intentional search, with a specific goal. The Hebrew word from the Old Testament that it most often translates is "darash" (דָּרַשׁ), which also means to ask, consult, seek insistently — and also "bakash" (בָּקַשׁ), to seek, desire.
G1934.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and the epistles. It is first used to describe what worldly men seek: pagans seek food and clothing (Matthew 6:32, Luke 12:30), a wicked generation seeks a sign (Matthew 16:4). It is also used for what believers seek: Israel seeks righteousness (Romans 11:7), the Hebrews seek a heavenly homeland (Hebrews 11:14, Hebrews 13:14). The word can also apply to the search for a person: one seeks after Jesus (Luke 4:42) or after Peter (Acts 12:19). In all these uses, it carries the idea of an active and directed quest.
G1934.portee: This word reminds the reader that seeking defines human life — we all seek something. The contrast that the Bible establishes is instructive: pagans seek material goods, while believers are called to seek the Kingdom and the heavenly homeland. It is a call to examine our own desires and aspirations: what are we really seeking? Is it the temporal or the eternal? The presence of the word in Hebrews encourages the believer not to forget that they are on their way to a better dwelling than this one.

sens: Destined to be put to death
Doomed to death, with no hope of escape
G1935.detail:
1. This word designates someone who has been legally or officially condemned to be executed — one who awaits death as a sentence. It is a pronounced judgment, an effective condemnation.
2. In Paul, the word takes on a figurative dimension: the apostles are like condemned men who are publicly displayed before their execution. In 1 Corinthians 4:9, Paul describes the apostles exposed "as a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men" — treated as the last of men, doomed to suffering and humiliation, without protection or honor.
G1935.origine: The word is composed of two elements: "epi" (toward, upon) and "thanatios" (related to death). The root evokes everything related to death, to the death sentence. The word paints the image of a person upon whom death weighs — one toward whom death is directed.
G1935.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 4:9. Paul uses it to metaphorically describe the condition of the apostles: they are treated like criminals condemned to death, displayed before the people, angels, and God Himself. This comparison illustrates the contempt, weakness, and vulnerability to which the apostles are subjected because of their faithfulness to the Gospel.
G1935.portee: This word invites the Christian to see how Paul reinterprets apostolic suffering not as a defeat, but as an imitation of Christ — delivered to death for our salvation. It is a call to accept humiliation and fragility as the path of authentic faith, and not to seek the honor or security of the world.

sens: The action of placing hands on someone
The gesture by which a gift, ability, or spiritual authority is conferred
The ordination or consecration of a person to a ministry
G1936.detail:
1. In the literal sense, it is simply the act of placing hands on a person. Simon notes in Acts 8:18 that "the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands": he sees the apostles placing their hands on other believers.
2. This gesture signifies the transmission of grace, a gift, or a spiritual ability. In 1 Timothy 4:14, Timothy is urged not to neglect the gift received through the laying on of the elders' hands: this simple physical contact accompanies the action of the Spirit that gives or confirms a charisma.
3. The laying on of hands constitutes an act of ordination or consecration.
